items.value: John Clarke - the 2025 Physics laureate who was born in the UK and holds a professorship at an American university
items.reasoning: The stem imposes two conditions at once: born in the UK, and working at an American university when the 2025 prize was announced. John Clarke was born in Cambridge, England, and is a professor of physics at the University of California, Berkeley; he shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics with Michel Devoret and John Martinis for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in an electric circuit. Each distractor fails exactly one condition: Michel Devoret works in the United States but was born in Paris; Richard Robson (Chemistry 2025, metal-organic frameworks) was born in England but has spent his career at the University of Melbourne in Australia; Joel Mokyr (Economic Sciences 2025) is at Northwestern University in the United States but was born in the Netherlands.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct - the four majors do share a governance structure, but they are not open for entry to every internationally ranked player over 14
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: although the four majors are owned and staged by four different national associations, they operate a shared governance structure - the Grand Slam Board, which frames the common Grand Slam Rule Book - so a formal partnership between the four does exist. Statement 2 is the absolute that fails: entry to a Grand Slam is governed by ranking cut-offs for direct acceptance, then qualifying, then a small number of wild cards, and the ITF age eligibility rule additionally restricts how many professional events a player aged 14 to 17 may play, so the events are not open to all internationally ranked players above 14. RUNNER-UP: D (1, 2 and 3). Statement 3 is the pivot, and it would win if the examiner is reading the per-player wild-card caps in the age eligibility rule as a 'limitation on the number of wild cards a player may receive' - the ordinary limit of eight wild cards is on the tournament, not on the player. Note the option set contains no '1 and 3 only', so if statement 3 is correct and statement 2 is not, the item has no defensible option; the absence of that combination is itself the strongest evidence for C.

items.value: The HCL-Foxconn joint venture semiconductor unit is in Uttar Pradesh (Jewar), not Madhya Pradesh - so that pair is wrongly matched
items.reasoning: The HCL-Foxconn joint venture display-driver chip plant approved under the India Semiconductor Mission is sited at Jewar in the Yamuna Expressway industrial area of Uttar Pradesh, so pairing it with Madhya Pradesh is wrong and C is the answer to a 'not correctly matched' question. The other three pairs hold: the CG Power unit with Renesas Electronics and Stars Microelectronics is an assembly and test facility at Sanand in Gujarat; Tata Semiconductor Assembly and Test Pvt. Ltd. is the outsourced assembly and test plant at Jagiroad in Assam; and SicSem Pvt. Ltd. is the silicon-carbide compound semiconductor unit at Bhubaneswar in Odisha.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct - the Bharat Forecast System targets panchayat-cluster-level forecasts, but it was developed by IITM Pune, not IIT Delhi
items.reasoning: Statement 2 is plainly wrong and settles the item: the Bharat Forecast System was built by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune, an autonomous institute under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, and is run operationally by the India Meteorological Department - IIT Delhi had no role. Statement 1 is correct: the model's headline claim is its very fine six-kilometre grid, and the purpose of that resolution is to move weather forecasting down from block level to the panchayat-cluster level so that warnings can be issued for a village neighbourhood rather than a district. That leaves A.

items.value: All three are correct - 'Boong', directed by Lakshmipriya Devi, won the BAFTA in the Children's and Family Film category and is the first Indian film to do so
items.reasoning: Statement 2 is certain: 'Boong' is the Manipuri-language feature directed by Lakshmipriya Devi, which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival. Statements 1 and 3 stand or fall together in a way that removes two options outright - statement 3 asserts that this is the FIRST Indian film to win in the category, which presupposes that it won, so options B and D, which accept statement 3 while rejecting statement 1, are internally incoherent and cannot be the intended answer. The contest is therefore A against C, and it turns entirely on whether the win was a first for India; that 'first Indian film' framing is precisely the news hook that makes the win examinable at all, so A. RUNNER-UP: C (1 and 2 only), which wins if some earlier Indian film had already taken this BAFTA category. Flagging honestly that this is a recall-dependent current-affairs item sitting at the edge of what I can verify from the stem, which is why it is not marked HIGH.

items.value: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; statement 3 is wrong because the description given - a blend of public and private with selective access - defines a hybrid blockchain, not a consortium blockchain
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is a fair statement of blockchain's combination of transparency and immutability: the ledger can be exposed to permitted stakeholders while the records themselves cannot be quietly rewritten. Statement 2 describes distributed ledger replication - every participating node holds a full copy and the copies reconcile almost immediately. Statement 4 states immutability: cryptographic hash-chaining means altering an accepted record would break every subsequent block, so a recorded entry cannot be changed or deleted. Statement 3 misnames a category: a consortium (or federated) blockchain is one governed jointly by a group of known organisations, whereas the 'blend of public and private, with selective data access' is the standard definition of a HYBRID blockchain. RUNNER-UP: D (1 and 4 only), which wins if the examiner treats 'syncing within seconds' in statement 2 as inaccurate, since block confirmation on major public chains takes minutes rather than seconds. The item reduces to C versus D on that single phrase; there is no option combining 1, 3 and 4, which confirms statement 2 is the intended pivot.

items.value: The dropshipping model - the seller sets prices but holds no inventory and passes orders to a supplier who ships direct to the customer
items.reasoning: The stem is a textbook definition of dropshipping: the retailer never takes possession of the goods, but keeps control of pricing and the customer relationship, forwarding order and shipping details to a third-party supplier who despatches to the buyer directly. The distractors describe different revenue models: an affiliate earns a commission for referring buyers to someone else's site and does not set the price; a transaction fee model earns a cut on each transaction processed on the platform; and an agency model earns a fee for acting on a principal's behalf. Only dropshipping combines pricing control with zero inventory and supplier-direct shipment.

items.value: The RBI's Financial Inclusion Index is built on three sub-indices: Access, Usage and Quality
items.reasoning: The RBI's FI-Index is a single composite number on a 0 to 100 scale built from three parameters - Access, weighted 35 per cent; Usage, weighted 45 per cent; and Quality, weighted 20 per cent - with Quality capturing financial literacy, consumer protection and inequalities in service. The other options mix in things the index does not use as top-level sub-indices: GDP contribution is not a financial-inclusion parameter at all, and while financial literacy does feature, it sits inside Quality rather than standing as a sub-index of its own.

items.value: ONDC aims to break the dominance of large e-commerce platforms by making digital commerce interoperable across networks
items.reasoning: ONDC unbundles e-commerce into open, interoperable protocols so that a buyer on one application can transact with a seller registered on a different one, instead of each large platform locking buyers and sellers into its own closed silo. That is exactly what option C states. A and B misread the initiative as state control or nationalisation of e-commerce, whereas ONDC is a set of open protocols on which private players are expected to build and compete; and D confuses ONDC with UPI, which is a separate payments rail - ONDC does not mandate any particular payment method.

items.value: The incorrect statement is that liability lies with users and their banks in both cases - for the Digital Rupee the liability is the Reserve Bank's, since CBDC is a direct central bank liability
items.reasoning: The Digital Rupee is sovereign currency in digital form and, like a banknote, is a direct liability of the Reserve Bank of India; a bank merely distributes it and holds it in a wallet. UPI, by contrast, moves commercial bank deposit money, which is a liability of the depositor's bank. So statement D, which asserts the same bank-side liability for both, is the one that is not correct. The other three are accurate: A correctly contrasts a real-time payment system with a digital form of sovereign paper currency; B correctly notes that UPI involves an actual debit and credit of bank accounts whereas a CBDC transfer simply moves value from one wallet to another with no interbank settlement leg for the end user; and C follows from B, since wallet-to-wallet CBDC transfers are not routed through and so are not reflected in bank account statements.

items.value: All three are correct - tokenization converts real-world assets into blockchain tokens, gives round-the-clock access aiding financial inclusion, and opens high-growth investment opportunities to individual investors
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is the definition itself and cannot be faulted: real-world asset tokenization records ownership of a physical or financial asset as a digital token on a blockchain. Statement 2 follows from the technology - blockchain settlement runs continuously rather than on exchange hours, so tokenized assets are tradable round the clock (24 x 7), and that continuous access combined with fractional ownership is the standard financial-inclusion argument made for the technology. Statement 3 is the fractional-ownership argument stated for India: by splitting a high-value asset such as commercial real estate or infrastructure into small tokens, opportunities previously confined to institutions and high-net-worth investors become reachable by retail investors. RUNNER-UP: C (1 and 2 only), which wins if the examiner treats statement 3 as an unproven forward claim given that tokenized RWAs are not yet a regulated retail product in India. Marked MED because both 2 and 3 are benefit claims rather than facts derivable from the stem.

items.value: A sustainability bond - one whose proceeds finance a combination of both green (environmental) and social projects
items.reasoning: Under the widely used ICMA taxonomy the label is decided by what the proceeds fund: a Green Bond funds environmental projects only, a Social Bond funds social projects only, and a Sustainability Bond is defined precisely as one whose proceeds are applied to finance or refinance a combination of both green and social projects - which is the stem word for word. A Sovereign Bond is not in this taxonomy at all; it is classified by who issues it, namely the government, and says nothing about the use of proceeds.

items.value: Only statement 2 is correct - M1xchange is a TReDS platform that discounts MSME invoices and bills of exchange; it neither lends against collateral nor rates credit
items.reasoning: M1xchange is one of the RBI-licensed Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) platforms, an electronic marketplace where an MSME supplier's invoices and bills of exchange drawn on large buyers are auctioned to financiers and discounted, so statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is wrong on the defining feature of TReDS: the financing is against the receivable itself and is collateral-free and without recourse to the MSME, which is the entire point of the mechanism. Statement 3 is wrong because credit rating is a distinct, separately registered activity performed by SEBI-registered credit rating agencies; a TReDS platform hosts the auction and does not rate anyone.

items.value: Crowding out is where heavy government borrowing pushes interest rates up and thereby reduces private investment
items.reasoning: When the government finances a deficit by borrowing, it competes with private borrowers for the same pool of loanable funds; the increased demand for funds raises interest rates, and dearer credit makes some private investment projects unviable, so private investment falls. That displacement of private spending by public borrowing is the crowding-out effect, as stated in B. Option A describes the opposite phenomenon, crowding in, where public spending raises demand and complements private investment; C reverses the effect of taxation on private investible surplus; and D describes fiscal policy having no demand effect at all, which is a different proposition altogether.

items.value: Only statements 1 and 3 are correct - India is not the second-largest REE miner after China, and rare earth elements number seventeen, not thirteen
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: rare earths are central to permanent magnets, sensors, lasers and optics, and so underpin AI hardware, robotics and space technology. Statement 3 is correct: the National Critical Mineral Mission was approved by the Union Cabinet in January 2025 to build a secure and self-reliant critical mineral supply chain covering exploration, mining, processing and recycling. Statement 2 is false - China dominates REE mining by a very wide margin, but India is not the second-largest producer; its output is a small fraction of the global total and it ranks well below producers such as the United States, Myanmar and Australia, notwithstanding that India holds sizeable reserves. Statement 4 is false on the count: rare earth elements are a group of seventeen elements, the fifteen lanthanides together with scandium and yttrium, not thirteen. If statement 4 were read as correct the answer would instead be C, so that single number is the pivot of the item.

items.value: Both statements are correct - hull insurance covers the aircraft itself, and the Montreal Convention imposes strict liability on airlines for passenger death without proof of fault
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is the standard definition: aviation hull insurance covers physical loss of or damage to the aircraft as property - airframe, engines and installed on-board equipment - as distinct from liability cover for passengers and third parties. Statement 2 is also correct: the Montreal Convention of 1999, to which India and well over a hundred other states are party, replaced the older fault-based Warsaw regime with a two-tier scheme in which the carrier is strictly liable up to a defined SDR limit for death or bodily injury of a passenger, so the family or nominee need not prove negligence to recover that first tier; only beyond that limit can the carrier attempt to escape liability by disproving fault.

items.value: Both statements are correct - crowdfunding is the solicitation of small sums from many investors via a web platform for a specific project, and it lets SMEs raise funds cheaply without rigorous procedures
items.reasoning: Statement 1 reproduces the standard regulatory description of crowdfunding: raising small amounts of money from a large number of contributors through an internet-based platform or social networking site, for a specific project, business venture or social cause. Statement 2 states the advantage usually cited alongside it: because the route sidesteps the disclosure, intermediation and listing formalities of a conventional public issue or a bank loan appraisal, small and medium enterprises and start-ups can access capital at a lower cost and with far less procedural burden - which is also precisely why regulators treat the route as carrying higher investor risk. Both being sound, the answer is C.

items.value: Rows 2 and 4 are fully correct - the L.C. Gupta Committee on derivatives under SEBI and the Malegam Committee on microfinance under the RBI
items.reasoning: Row 2 is correct throughout: SEBI constituted the L.C. Gupta Committee in 1996 to draw up the regulatory framework and roadmap for introducing derivatives trading in India. Row 4 is likewise correct: the RBI set up the Y.H. Malegam sub-committee of its Central Board to examine issues in the microfinance sector, and its recommendations shaped the NBFC-MFI regulatory framework. Row 1 fails on the third column: the R.N. Malhotra Committee on insurance reform was appointed by the Government of India in 1993, and it could not have been formed under the IRDAI because that regulator did not yet exist - the IRDA was itself created in 1999 on this committee's recommendation. Row 3 fails on the second column: the Urjit Patel Committee, though correctly placed under the RBI, was constituted to revise and strengthen the monetary policy framework, not to reform bank lending to the housing sector.

items.value: Only statements 1 and 4 are correct - NBFCs cannot take demand deposits and their depositors get no DICGC cover; but not all NBFCs register with the RBI, and they are outside the payment and settlement system
items.reasoning: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are the three classic differences between a bank and an NBFC: an NBFC cannot accept demand deposits, it is not part of the payment and settlement system so it cannot issue cheques drawn on itself, and deposit insurance from the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation is not available to depositors of NBFCs. That makes 1 and 4 correct and 3 incorrect as stated. Statement 2 is the other error: registration with the RBI is not universal, because categories of NBFC regulated by another authority are exempted - insurance companies under the IRDAI, stock broking and merchant banking entities under SEBI, chit fund companies under state legislation, and nidhi companies under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Hence A.

items.value: Only statements 1 and 2 are correct - the MPI uses the Alkire-Foster method and NITI Aayog's index has twelve indicators; maternal health and bank account are India-specific additions, not indicators shared with the UNDP index
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: both the global and the national multidimensional poverty indices are computed by the Alkire-Foster dual cut-off method, which identifies the deprived and then multiplies the headcount ratio by the intensity of deprivation. Statement 2 is correct: NITI Aayog's National MPI keeps the three dimensions of health, education and standard of living but expands the indicator set to twelve. Statement 3 inverts the actual position - the UNDP's global MPI uses ten indicators, and maternal health and bank account are two of the additional indicators that NITI Aayog added to reflect national priorities, so far from being common to both they are precisely the indicators that distinguish the national index from the global one.
